newsitem.title: FRANCE: Parliament backs down over television quotas.
newsitem.headline: Parliament backs down over television quotas.

text.p: The European Parliament abandoned on Tuesday its long-standing demands for stricter limits on the number of Hollywood programmes shown on European television, sidestepping a showdown with member states.

A large majority of Euro-MPs demanded in the second reading that a rule in the television without frontiers directive 89/EEC/552 that 51 percent of Europe's screentime should be devoted to European works should be made mandatory by erasing the words "where practicable".
But the idea failed to secure the qualified majority of 314 votes needed to force the Council to go to conciliation.
When it made the demand in the first reading a simple majority was enough.
The vote brings to an end one of the EU's longest-running sagas, killing off deputies hopes of revising the directive to brake Hollywood's domination of the EU's television screens.

"Very powerful interests have won today," British Socialist deputy Carole Tongue, a member of the parliament's Culture Committee, told Reuters, pointing to the United States' $6 billion trade surplus with the EU in the audiovisual sector.
"It is a major defeat for the European audiovisual industry," she said.

Luciana Castellina, chairwoman of the Culture Committee who has led the fight for tougher limits on Hollywood, said the fact that member states could ignore the wishes of well over half the EU assembly, showed a power imbalance in the bloc and that powers of co-decision gained under the Maastricht Treaty meant nothing.
The parliament had effectively been fighting a losing battle with the Culture Council who had made clear in advance it had no intention of curbing the prime U.S. export industry.

But despite a convergence of views in the Culture Committee between different political groups, on Tuesday deputies from the European People's Party accepted free trade arguments advanced by the European commercial television sector and swayed the vote in favour of Hollywood.
"The interests which are represented in this conflict are very heavy," a downcast Castellina told a news conference.
With the prospect of stricter quotas, Hollywood and the European commercial television industry set up high pressure lobbying bases in Brussels.

Former French Culture Minister and French Socialist Deputy Jack Lang, whose country led a lone fight against other EU countries for stricter controls on U.S. culture, said Hollywood could sleep safely after the vote.
"Washington can be reassured. Whether it comes to Zaire or culture the majority of Europeans lie down when America tells them to," he said in a statement.
The parliament stuck by two other key demands which will now be hammered out with EU governments and the European Commission in conciliation.
It will press demands for all new television sets to be equipped within a year with a so-called V-chip, which would allow parents to screen out violent programmes from their children.
A spokesman for Culture Commissioner Marcelino Oreja said the demand was unrealistic as the technology would not be available in time.
It will also press for rules to ensure that ordinary people can watch major sports events like the world cup, even if pay-television channels secure exclusive rights to broadcast them.
But the parliament decided not to demand tougher rules for advertising and teleshopping, so the rules laid down in the Council's Common Position will apply.
